result: HCC is a major global health burden, being the most common liver tumor type, a leading cause of cancer-related deaths, with increasing worldwide incidence. In China specifically, primary liver cancer ranks as the fourth most common malignant tumor and second leading cause of cancer-related deaths.
evaluation: Claims C1-C3 and C12-C13 present epidemiological facts about HCC that are well-established in the literature and supported by the cited references (Sung et al., 2021; Llovet et al., 2021b; Villanueva, 2019). These are standard knowledge claims in the field with appropriate citations.

result: Most HCC patients are not candidates for curative surgery due to disease progression, with approximately 50-60% requiring systemic therapy. Kinase inhibitor therapy with sorafenib and lenvatinib has been the main treatment for advanced HCC for over a decade, achieving median overall survival of 11-14 months.
evaluation: Claims C4-C6 and C14-C16 accurately describe the treatment landscape for HCC, including the limited applicability of curative surgery and the historical role of kinase inhibitors. These are well-established clinical facts supported by standard practice and literature.

result: Immunotherapy with immune checkpoint inhibitors has revolutionized HCC treatment, with combination therapy proving more effective than sorafenib. Combining anti-PD-L1/PD-1 and CTLA-4 antibodies with anti-VEGF bevacizumab extends median survival to 19 months.
evaluation: Claims C7-C8 and C17 are supported by cited clinical trial data (Llovet et al., 2021a; Llovet et al., 2018; Finn et al., 2020; Qin et al., 2021). The 19-month median survival figure for combination therapy represents a significant improvement over historical controls and is documented in the referenced studies.

result: Despite progress in immunotherapy, molecular mechanisms remain unclear and immune resistance is challenging to overcome. The complex intercellular communication network in the HCC immune microenvironment regulates tumor escape and drug resistance.
evaluation: Claims C9-C11 and C167 accurately characterize the current state of knowledge regarding immunotherapy resistance in HCC. The acknowledgment of incomplete mechanistic understanding and the role of the tumor microenvironment is appropriate and reflects the rationale for the review.

result: The liver maintains systemic homeostasis through high immune tolerance to foreign antigens, particularly those of intestinal origin. Key immunosuppressive cells in HCC include Tregs, MDSCs, TAMs, TANs, and DCs.
evaluation: Claims C18-C19 present established immunological facts about liver physiology and the cellular composition of the HCC immune microenvironment, supported by appropriate citations (Llovet et al., 2022a; Llovet et al., 2022b).

result: During tumor immunity, T cells differentiate into exhausted CD8+ T cells (TEX) characterized by loss of cytokines, high expression of inhibitory markers (PD-1, Tim-3, LAG3, TIGIT, 2B4), and decreased proliferative potential. TOX is highly expressed in tumor-specific CD8+ T cells and its overexpression induces exhaustion. CD8+ T-cell depletion in TME is a primary cause of immunotherapy resistance, but this can be reversed by targeting PD-1 and CTLA-4.
evaluation: Claims C20-C27 describe well-established mechanisms of T-cell exhaustion with appropriate citations (Sen et al., 2016; Blackburn et al., 2009; Scott et al., 2019; Schietinger and Greenberg, 2014; Said et al., 2010). The role of TOX and the reversibility of exhaustion through checkpoint blockade are supported by the cited literature.

result: Regulatory T cells (Tregs) are characterized by CD25, CTLA-4, and Foxp3 expression and suppress anti-tumor immunity when accumulated in tumors. Treg subpopulations modulate CD8+ T-cell exhaustion through IL-10 and IL-35 secretion. Deletion of IL-10 or IL-35 in Tregs attenuates tumor growth and reduces TEX. The PD-1/PD-L1 pathway may link to IL-10 generation, and IL-10/IL-35 promote CD8+ T-cell exhaustion via the BLIMP-1 pathway.
evaluation: Claims C28-C34 present well-documented mechanisms of Treg-mediated immunosuppression with appropriate citations (Tay et al., 2023; Sawant et al., 2019; Ribas and Wolchok, 2018; Pauken and Wherry, 2015; Said et al., 2010; Turnis et al., 2016; Panduro et al., 2016). The experimental evidence from deletion studies supports the functional role of these cytokines.

result: Sequencing analysis shows decreased CTL/Treg ratio in HCC tissues, indicating a shift from activated to suppressed immune state. TGF-β promotes Treg production and inhibits CD8+ T cells; inhibition with SM-16 reduces Treg infiltration and causes tumor regression. CCR4+ Tregs acquire immunosuppressive stem-like properties through chromatin reprogramming, and CCR4 antagonists can overcome resistance. Single-cell sequencing of 29 HCC patients shows high Treg infiltration alongside PD-1+CD8+ T cells, and patient-derived Tregs suppress CD8+ T-cell function in co-culture.
evaluation: Claims C35-C41 are supported by cited studies providing sequencing data, functional assays, and therapeutic intervention results (Ally et al., 2017; Shen et al., 2015; Gao et al., 2022; Magen et al., 2023; Fu et al., 2007). The convergence of evidence from multiple approaches strengthens these findings.

result: MDSCs are immature, heterogeneous bone marrow-derived cells categorized into PMN-MDSCs and M-MDSCs with distinct surface markers in mice and humans. PMN-MDSCs are recruited via CXC chemokines (CXCL1, CXCL2, CXCL5), M-MDSCs via CCL2-CCR2 axis, and CCR5 ligands recruit both subsets.
evaluation: Claims C42-C47 accurately describe MDSC classification and recruitment mechanisms with appropriate citations (Bronte et al., 2016; Groth et al., 2021; Lim et al., 2020; Blattner et al., 2018). These are well-established characterizations in the field.

result: MDSCs exert immunosuppression through multiple mechanisms: upregulating TAM RTKs, expressing IDO/ARG1 to expand Tregs, depleting amino acids (L-arginine, cysteine) needed for T-cell activation, producing NO that interferes with T-cell signaling, secreting IL-10 to suppress DCs and promote Tregs, interacting with PD-1 receptors, undergoing ferroptosis to release oxidized lipids, and releasing EVs that inhibit NK cells. PMN-MDSCs express ARG1 and ROS, while M-MDSCs express TGF-β, IL-10, and PD-L1. HIF-1α upregulation enhances M-MDSC differentiation into TAMs.
evaluation: Claims C48-C59 describe well-documented MDSC immunosuppressive mechanisms with extensive citations (Holtzhausen et al., 2019; Yu et al., 2013; Zoso et al., 2014; Srivastava et al., 2010; Lu et al., 2019; Lee-Chang et al., 2019; Bodogai et al., 2015; van Vlerken-Ysla et al., 2023; Kwak et al., 2020; Tumino et al., 2021; Burke et al., 2014; Gabrilovich, 2017; Gabrilovich et al., 2012; Veglia et al., 2021). The diversity of mechanisms is well-supported.

result: TAMs are categorized into TAM1 (FOLR2+), TAM2 (SPP1+), and TAM3 (MT1G+) subsets. TCGA analysis shows TAMs correlate with poor prognosis, likely due to inhibiting T-cell recognition and killing of tumor cells. In hypoxic TME, macrophage SPP1 upregulation interacts with CAFs to form a tumor immune barrier (TIB) structure; SPP1 blockade or knockdown breaks this barrier and sensitizes tumors to immunotherapy. CSF1 and CCL2 recruit monocytes that differentiate into M2 macrophages. TAM-like features (APOE, C1QA, C1QB, TREM2, SLC40A1, GPNMB expression) associate with poor prognosis. In liver tumor metastasis models, Fas+CD8+ T cells undergo apoptosis after interacting with FasL+ macrophages, creating an 'immune desert'. PLVAP ECs, CD163 macrophages, and TIGIT Tregs are enriched in tumor tissues.
evaluation: Claims C60-C68 present TAM characterization and functional data supported by multiple citations (Sharma et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2019a; Condamine et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2023; Kang et al., 2011; Eggert et al., 2016; Li et al., 2017; Lavin et al., 2017; Yu et al., 2021; Rantakari et al., 2016). The TIB concept (C63-C64) is particularly notable as it represents the authors' own previous work, which is appropriately cited.

result: TAMs facilitate tumor progression and metastasis through JAK2/STAT3/miR-506-3p/FoxQ1 signaling. The Hedgehog signaling pathway is involved in TAM polarization toward M2; tumor cells secrete sonic hedgehog driving M2 polarization and produce CXCL9/CXCL10 inhibiting CD8 T-cell recruitment. TAMs secrete VEGF-α to facilitate stromal angiogenesis and HCC progression.
evaluation: Claims C69-C72 describe TAM-mediated tumor promotion mechanisms with appropriate citations (Wei et al., 2019; Banerjee et al., 2023). These represent established pathways in the field.

result: Several therapeutic strategies target TAMs: M2pep selectively targets M2 macrophages without affecting M1; zoledronic acid reverses TAM polarity from M2 to M1 by reducing IL-10, VEGF, MMP9 and restoring iNOS; CP-870,893 (CD40 agonist) repolarizes TAMs to M1 and induces macrophage-dependent tumor regression in mice; AXL is a top drug target for overcoming ICI resistance; emactuzumab (anti-CSF-1R) decreases TAMs in tumor lesions; VEGF antagonists induce vascular normalization and remodel TAM phenotype.
evaluation: Claims C73-C80 describe therapeutic approaches with supporting citations (Kakoschky et al., 2018; Ngambenjawong et al., 2016; Cieslewicz et al., 2013; Comito et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2021; Li et al., 2022; Jiang et al., 2021; Ries et al., 2014; DeNardo and Ruffell, 2019; Mantovani et al., 2017). However, the clinical translation of these approaches remains limited as noted in the text.

result: TAN infiltration positively correlates with poor prognosis. TANs exist as anti-tumorigenic (N1) or protumorigenic (N2) phenotypes. N2 TANs form neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) that support tumor growth. CAFs inhibit neutrophil function via SDF-1α/CXCR4/IL-6 pathway and secrete CLCF1 mediating CXCL6 and TGF-β expression for neutrophil recruitment and N2 polarization. N2 neutrophils induce stem cell phenotype in HCC cells and promote CXCL5 secretion. Dysregulated neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio strongly associates with HCC prognosis, possibly due to neutrophil TGF-β release affecting immune regulation and angiogenesis.
evaluation: Claims C81-C87 describe TAN biology and function with appropriate citations (Coffelt et al., 2016; Cheng et al., 2018; Arvanitakis et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2012; Gonzalez-Sanchez et al., 2021). The N1/N2 paradigm and NET formation are well-established concepts.

result: DCs are important APCs with migratory properties that present antigens in tissues and lymph nodes. CD8+ T-cell activation depends on early DC activation by CD4+ T helper cells through immune synapse formation. Cancer cells escape immunity by expressing inhibitory ligands (PD-1, CTLA-4, LAG3, TIM3) that disrupt the immune synapse. HCC patients show reduced circulating pDCs and cDCs with lower co-stimulatory molecule expression. BDCA2+ pDCs in tumors associate with high AFP, advanced staging, and increased Treg/IL-17-producing cell infiltration. pDCs induce CD4+ T-cell differentiation into IL-10-producing Tr1 cells in vitro. Tumor cDCs express inhibitory ligands (PD-L1, Gal9, MHC-II, CD86, CD80).
evaluation: Claims C88-C95 describe DC biology and dysfunction in HCC with appropriate citations (Heras-Murillo et al., 2024; Jenne and Kubes, 2013; McLane et al., 2019; Pirillo et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2017; Sun et al., 2021). The data on DC alterations in HCC patients is well-documented.

result: DC-based immunotherapy shows promise: a meta-analysis indicates DC-based therapy improves CD4+/CD8+ T-cell ratio with safety. DC-OK432 produces Th1 cytokines (IL-12, IFN-γ) and enhances cytotoxic T-cell activity via CD40/CD40L, effective in combination therapy. Mouse HCC models treated with DC vaccine plus PD-1 inhibitor show longer OS and reduced tumor volume.
evaluation: Claims C96-C98 present evidence for DC-based therapeutic approaches with appropriate citations (Chen et al., 2018; Nakamoto et al., 2011; Teng et al., 2021; Nakai and Matsumura, 2021). The preclinical and clinical data support the potential of these approaches, though clinical translation remains limited.

result: CAFs upregulate multiple markers (α-SMA, FAP, FSP1, PDGFR-α/β, vimentin). While a small subset may restrict tumor growth, the majority promote tumor cell proliferation. CAFs maintain ECM homeostasis by synthesizing and secreting ECM proteins under pathological conditions. Hypoxic TME regulates ECM remodeling by CAFs, with HIF-1α-expressing CAFs promoting tumorigenesis and metastasis. TGF-β is the most thoroughly studied CAF paracrine pathway.
evaluation: Claims C99-C103 describe CAF characteristics and functions with appropriate citations (Giraldo et al., 2019; Barrett and Puré, 2020; Mizutani et al., 2019; Fiori et al., 2019; Hinshaw and Shevde, 2019; Joshi et al., 2021; Miles and Sikes, 2014; Calvo et al., 2013; Gilkes et al., 2014; Mariathasan et al., 2018). These are well-established features of CAF biology.

result: A strong association exists between stem cell-like properties and mesenchymal-like tumor cell phenotype. Cancer cells undergoing EMT acquire stem cell-like traits facilitated by TGF-β upregulation and SPP1 secretion. Patients with heightened TGF-β, MAPK, and PI3K/Akt expression exhibit disease progression and poor prognosis. CAFs influence tumor angiogenesis through VEGF and PDGF upregulation, secrete CXCL12 to recruit endothelial progenitors, and mediate protease upregulation (COX2, CXCL1, CXCL2, CYR61/CCN1, IL-1β, IL-6, osteopontin) via NF-κB to promote tumor growth, macrophage recruitment, and vasculature formation. CAF-secreted CLCF1 mediates CXCL6 and TGF-β expression for neutrophil recruitment and N2 polarization.
evaluation: Claims C104-C110 describe CAF-mediated tumor promotion mechanisms with appropriate citations (Morel et al., 2012; Todaro et al., 2014; Fessler et al., 2016; Heldin et al., 2012; Calon et al., 2015; Fukumura et al., 1998; Feig et al., 2013; Erez et al., 2010; Colak and Ten Dijke, 2017). These represent well-documented CAF functions.

result: Cancer cells manipulate their microenvironment by modulating immune cells and ECM. The PD-L1/PD-1 pathway is exploited for immune evasion. M2 macrophages shape tumor stroma by secreting growth factors (FGF, PDGF-β) and TGF-β, triggering fibroblast activation and collagen deposition. Macrophages emerge as critical TME orchestrators, inducing myofibroblast differentiation, fostering fibrosis, and sustaining stromal cell viability.
evaluation: Claims C111-C114 describe tumor-microenvironment interactions with appropriate citations (van Niel et al., 2022; Lucotti et al., 2022; Dhanasekaran et al., 2016; Llovet et al., 2016). These are well-established concepts in tumor biology.

result: CD8+ T-cell depletion in TME is a primary impediment to immunotherapy. Disease progression in HCC correlates with PD-1high CD8+ T-cell enrichment in TME. Targeting immune checkpoints (PD-L1, TIM-3, LAG-3) with ICIs can reverse T-cell exhaustion. However, sustained IFN-I signaling exacerbates terminal CD8+ T-cell exhaustion, leading to ICI resistance and poor prognosis. Combined anti-PD-1 and anti-IFNAR-1 therapy significantly prolonged survival in mouse HCC models, while either alone failed.
evaluation: Claims C115-C119 describe mechanisms of immunotherapy resistance and potential solutions with appropriate citations (Ma et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2022a). The finding that IFN-I can paradoxically promote resistance (C118-C119) is particularly important and supported by experimental data showing benefit of combined blockade.

result: MDSCs contribute to immunotherapy resistance through multiple mechanisms: producing MMP9, with CARD9 regulating tumor growth by modulating IDO; secreting cytokines (IL-6, IL-10, IL-23) promoting cell survival; releasing EVs with increased PD-L1 and TGF-β; depleting L-arginine via high ARG1 levels impairing T-cell function; producing iNOS and NOX2 inducing oxidative stress; releasing NO and peroxynitrite that reduce endothelial adhesion molecules and disrupt chemokine-mediated T-cell recruitment; and inhibiting NK cell IFN-γ and TNF expression through NO generation.
evaluation: Claims C120-C126 describe MDSC-mediated resistance mechanisms with appropriate citations (Wu et al., 2019a; De Veirman et al., 2019; Lin et al., 2019; Fleming et al., 2019; Iwata et al., 2016; Feng et al., 2018; Fiaschi and Chiarugi, 2012; Gehad et al., 2012; Stiff et al., 2018). These represent well-documented immunosuppressive mechanisms.

result: TAMs contribute to immunotherapy resistance by expressing immune inhibitory receptors (PD-L1/2, CD80/CD86) causing T-cell depletion. PD-L1/PD-1 interaction inhibits TCR signaling, inducing T-cell exhaustion. TAMs secrete immunosuppressive factors (VISTA, TGF-β, IDO) and reshape TME. TAMs upregulate SPP1 in hypoxic microenvironments, interacting with CAFs to form a 'TIB' that weakens immunotherapy efficacy. Angiopoietin-2 links TAMs to anti-VEGF escape capability. Sustained glycolytic activation in TAMs may deprive immune effector cells of glucose. TAMs expressing high Fcγ receptors sequester immune checkpoint blockers, preventing target interaction. PD-1 therapy-induced T-cell activation increases CSF1 secretion, promoting M2 TAM polarization as a resistance determinant.
evaluation: Claims C127-C134 describe TAM-mediated resistance mechanisms with appropriate citations (Chen et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2020; Hmeljak et al., 2018; Llosa et al., 2015; Hashimoto et al., 2016; Coffelt et al., 2010; Mantovani et al., 2017; Chang et al., 2015; Arlauckas et al., 2017; Neubert et al., 2018). The TIB concept (C130) represents the authors' previous work. The finding about checkpoint blocker sequestration (C133) and CSF1-mediated resistance (C134) are particularly important mechanistic insights.

result: TANs contribute to immunoresistance in HCC by releasing cytokines (HGF, oncostatin M, β2-integrin, neutrophil elastase, MMP9, VEGF) and secreting chemokines (CCL2, CCL17) that recruit macrophages to tumor sites. TAN depletion significantly augments sorafenib efficacy in murine models. A single-cell neutrophil atlas revealed higher prevalence of CD10+ALPL+ neutrophils in anti-PD-1-resistant patients; these neutrophils exhibit an immunosuppressive phenotype by promoting irreversible T-cell exhaustion and reducing cytotoxicity, originating from tumor cell reprogramming.
evaluation: Claims C135-C140 describe TAN-mediated resistance with appropriate citations (Kuang et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2016; De Bock et al., 2011; Meng et al., 2023). The identification of CD10+ALPL+ neutrophils as a resistance marker (C139-C140) represents an important recent finding supported by single-cell analysis.

result: In liver fibrosis context, increased NETs in tumor-associated ECM together with collagen type I enveloping tumor cells hinder physical contact with cytotoxic T cells, impairing ICI response. Shield-like structures formed by NETs and Col1 around HCC cells trap and deplete activated T cells through proteases and immunosuppressive molecules on NET chromatin scaffolds. The synergistic action of liver fibrosis-associated ECM, Col1, and NETs prevents distant T-cell infiltration into tumor areas, creating regions enriched in neutrophils/NETs but depleted of T cells.
evaluation: Claims C141-C143 describe NET-mediated resistance mechanisms with appropriate citations (Schauer et al., 2014; Kaltenmeier et al., 2021). The concept of NETs forming physical and biochemical barriers to T-cell infiltration is well-supported and represents an important mechanism linking liver fibrosis to immunotherapy resistance.

result: Under steady-state conditions without pro-inflammatory stimuli, DC activation of T cells results in T-cell tolerance. Dysfunction in DC-mediated antigen presentation and subsequent T-cell suppression constitute core mechanisms underlying immune evasion in HCC.
evaluation: Claims C144-C145 describe DC-mediated immune evasion with appropriate citations (Jones et al., 2016; Barry et al., 2018). These represent established concepts in tumor immunology.

result: Two distinct CAF subsets exist: inflammatory CAFs and myofibroblastic CAFs (myCAFs). Within myCAFs, ECM-myCAF and TGF-β-myCAF subgroups play critical roles in shaping immunosuppressive milieu and conferring immunotherapy resistance. ECM-myCAFs stimulate PD-1 and CTLA-4 expression on CD4+CD25+ T lymphocytes, while PD-1+ CTLA-4+ Tregs reciprocally alter TGF-β-myCAF proportion by converting ECM-myCAFs. CAFs produce abundant collagen, potentially erecting physical barriers impeding adaptive immune cell migration to antigen-presenting sites.
evaluation: Claims C146-C149 describe CAF heterogeneity and resistance mechanisms with appropriate citations (Northey et al., 2017; Costa et al., 2018; Mariathasan et al., 2018). The identification of distinct CAF subsets and their reciprocal interactions with Tregs represents important mechanistic insight into resistance.

result: The BCLC staging system guides treatment selection based on tumor burden, liver function, performance status, and symptoms. Systemic therapy including immunotherapy is indicated for BCLC C stage patients. Clinical trials exploring adjuvant and neoadjuvant immunotherapies in early/intermediate-stage HCC show promising results. Neoadjuvant immunotherapies (nivolumab, ipilimumab, cemiplimab, cabozantinib) demonstrate encouraging outcomes with increased T-cell infiltration and pathological complete response rates. However, BCLC stage C patients consistently represent the majority (78-91%) in clinical trials.
evaluation: Claims C150-C154 describe the clinical staging system and trial landscape with appropriate citations (Topalian et al., 2019; Galle et al., 2018; Bruix et al., 2021). These accurately reflect current clinical practice and trial design.

result: Immunotherapy following locoregional treatments (tumor ablation, TACE, transarterial radioembolization) shows promise due to increased antigen presentation from tumor cell destruction. Tremelimumab immunotherapy shows increased tumor CD8+ T-cell infiltration in HCC patients, suggesting combination with subtotal ablation or TACE.
evaluation: Claims C155-C156 describe combination therapy approaches with appropriate citations (Gudd et al., 2021; Dolladille et al., 2020; Pinato et al., 2020; Nogueira et al., 2019). The rationale for combining locoregional therapy with immunotherapy is well-supported.

result: The IMbrave150 trial demonstrated that atezolizumab plus bevacizumab achieved significant improvements in overall and progression-free survival, with median OS not reached in the combination group versus 13.2 months with sorafenib. Analysis of 194 Chinese patients showed HR for OS of 0.44, suggesting 56% relative risk reduction and 6-month survival rate of 86.6%. The GO30140 trial showed ORR of 36% by RECIST 1.1 and 39% by HCC mRECIST, with median OS of 17.1 months and no new safety concerns.
evaluation: Claims C157-C159 present clinical trial results with appropriate citations (Cheng et al., 2022; Finn et al., 2020; Galle et al., 2021; Lee et al., 2020). The IMbrave150 trial represents a landmark study that changed clinical practice, and the data are accurately reported.

result: Multiple first-line clinical trials show varied results: ORIENT-32 demonstrated superior OS and PFS with sindilizumab plus bevacizumab over sorafenib (OS HR=0.569, PFS HR=0.567). CheckMate 459 did not show significant OS prolongation but reported higher ORR. KEYNOTE-524 revealed ORR of 46% by mRECIST and 36% by RECIST v1.1 with 83% target lesion reduction. RATIONALE 208 showed ORR of 13.6% and median OS of 13.5 months in second-line setting. KEYNOTE-240 demonstrated ORR of 18.3% and OS of 13.9 months. RESCUE study showed better anti-tumor activity and safety with karelizumab plus apatinib.
evaluation: Claims C160-C165 present clinical trial results with appropriate citations (Ren et al., 2021; Yau et al., 2022; Serrano et al., 2022; Ren et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2021). The data are accurately reported and represent the current state of clinical evidence. The variability in outcomes across trials is appropriately noted.

result: The HCC immune microenvironment comprises immune cells, fibroblasts, and stromal cells playing important roles in tumor cell proliferation, invasion, and angiogenesis. Resistance to immunotherapy in HCC is primarily due to the intricate regulatory network within the TME. Due to tumor heterogeneity, targeting the TME may be a more effective strategy than targeting tumor cells.
evaluation: Claims C166-C168 present the overall conclusions about the TME with appropriate citations (Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011; Lujambio et al., 2013; Zhu et al., 2022). These represent the central thesis of the review and are well-supported by the extensive evidence presented throughout the manuscript.
